lectures.title: How to choose a Linux Distribution?

cues.en: I want to finish this chapter with the Or by answering the question How should you use a Linux distribution?
And first of all, what I would recommend is that you write down the requirements.
What do you need?
So, for example, do you need commercial support?
If so, for how many years until you are ready to jump to the next version?
Are you willing to pay for a license here?
Do you need tools like Linux or do you use specific software that requires a specific distribution,
or are there any additional requirements?
As an example, maybe you want to deploy a NodeJS application and that relies on a recent version of
NodeJS, maybe one of the distributions still ships with an outdated version there, and it can't run
your software by default.
In that case, you would need to install a more recent version of NodeJS manually, but then maybe this
will later cause some dependency issues and maybe this might be a reason why you might prefer a different
Linux distribution so that you do not run into those problems.
Or maybe you are using a software from a specific vendor that's proprietary and the vendor is like,
Yeah, this software works perfectly only with, let's say for example, Red Hat, Enterprise Linux.
And in that case, if you wanted to rely on commercial support of that third party, you might be required
to actually use Red Hat Enterprise Linux in case you, let's say something breaks, you want to be able
to sue that other company or whatever is defined in that contract.
So those would be requirements that you would need to find out or that you would need to analyze when
you want to choose your Linux distribution.
